name: wolfSSL
workload: Full TLS 1.2/1.3 handshake and session-resumption throughput (new connections/sec, via HAProxy) under an independent third-party benchmark
claimed_speedup: In HAProxy's tests: full-handshake throughput ~48,000 conn/s for wolfSSL 5.7.0, roughly matching OpenSSL 1.1.1 (~48,000) and beating OpenSSL 3.1-3.4 (~42,500) and OpenSSL 3.0.x (~21,000); on TLS-resumption with standard pthread locks, wolfSSL scaled linearly to ~150,000 conn/s at 64 threads vs OpenSSL 1.1.1w collapsing to ~17,800 conn/s and OpenSSL 3.0.2 at only ~1,500-1,600 conn/s (~1% of wolfSSL's throughput)
compiler_and_flags: Not fully stated for wolfSSL specifically; article only documents that AWS-LC required -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 to enable atomics
hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge instance, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores
stars_or_usage: 2.9k stars; FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated, widely used in embedded/IoT/cloud TLS deployments
tradeoffs: GPLv3 licensing (commercial dual license available for proprietary use); embedded-focused footprint and API, with an OpenSSL compatibility layer for porting
caveats: Benchmark run and published by HAProxy (independent third party), not wolfSSL itself, so it is not a first-party claim; compiler and flags are not fully documented for every library tested; wolfSSL's own README separately claims 'dramatically better performance... over OpenSSL' with no numbers at all (a tier-D-only claim on its own).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "wolfssl" --sort stars; corroborating benchmark found via HN Algolia query "aws-lc performance" -> https://www.haproxy.com/blog/state-of-ssl-stacks

name: AWS-LC
workload: Full TLS 1.2/1.3 handshake and session-resumption throughput (new connections/sec, via HAProxy) under an independent third-party benchmark
claimed_speedup: AWS-LC 1.29.0 (built with -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11) reached ~63,000 conn/s in the full-handshake test, beating OpenSSL 3.1-3.4 (~42,500) and OpenSSL 3.0.x (~21,000), roughly matching/exceeding OpenSSL 1.1.1 (~48,000); in the TLS-resumption test with HAProxy's lightweight locks it was the best overall performer at ~183,000 conn/s vs OpenSSL 1.1.1w's 124,000 and OpenSSL 3.0.2/3.0.14's ~7,000-8,000 conn/s
compiler_and_flags: gcc; article documents that the default CMake config forces C99 (pthread locks) and that -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 must be set to enable atomics for full performance; exact gcc version/optimization flags not given
hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge instance, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores
stars_or_usage: 835 stars; used internally at AWS (s2n-tls, AWS SDKs, AWS-LC-rs) for TLS/crypto
tradeoffs: Code inherited from BoringSSL/OpenSSL retains original ISC/OpenSSL-era licensing alongside AWS-LC's own Apache-2.0/ISC files (mixed licensing across the tree); default build configuration silently underperforms until C11 is forced
caveats: Benchmark run and published by HAProxy (independent third party), not AWS; compiler version and optimization flags are not fully specified for every library in the comparison, only the C-standard build gotcha for AWS-LC.

name: Tempesta FW (Tempesta TLS)
workload: Server-side full and abbreviated TLS 1.2 handshakes (ECDHE+ECDSA over NIST P-256) measured with the project's own tls-perf tool and wrk, comparing Nginx 1.19.1/OpenSSL 1.1.1d against Tempesta FW's in-Linux-kernel TLS handshake implementation, on a 1-vCPU KVM VM and on 2-node bare-metal servers
claimed_speedup: 40-80% more TLS connections/sec than Nginx/OpenSSL and up to 4x lower latency in some tests; concretely: 1-CPU VM new-session RPS 2,180 vs 1,545 (+41%), avg latency 307ms vs 1,340ms (-77%); 2-CPU bare-metal session-resumption 35,263 vs 19,203 conn/s (+83%); 2-CPU bare-metal new-session RPS only 7,921 vs 7,426 (+6%). Raw crypto op/s were slower than OpenSSL: ECDSA 27,261 vs OpenSSL's 36,472 op/s, ECDHE 6,690 vs OpenSSL's 16,619 op/s -- the throughput win comes from avoiding user/kernel context switches and heap allocation, not from faster math.
hardware: 1 vCPU KVM VM on Intel Core i7-6500U host (no vAPIC), virtio_net; 2-node bare-metal cluster with Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 CPUs and Mellanox ConnectX-2 10GbE, Linux kernel 5.7 (also compared to 4.14)
tradeoffs: Linux-kernel-only (x86-64 with AVX/BMI/ADX required, no generic C fallback for the crypto routines), puts TLS handshake code in kernel space (larger attack surface / TCB), GPLv2 licensing, and the paper itself reports tail-latency spikes up to 30x worse in the worst case on bare metal under SoftIRQ load
caveats: This is a first-party paper/benchmark by the Tempesta Technologies team (NetDev 0x14 workshop paper), not independent peer review, so it is capped at tier C despite public benchmark code (tls-perf) and stated hardware; compiler and build flags are not given; the headline 40-80% figure applies mainly to the VM scenario and to session resumption -- the bare-metal new-session improvement was only +6%; test hardware and kernel (5.7, 2020) are dated.
